chunks.title: Classifying uveitis & reading the signs
chunks.tldr: Anatomic: anterior (commonest; acute, unilateral, pain, photophobia, ciliary flush, small pupil), intermediate (vitritis, snowballs/snowbanks), posterior (retinitis, choroiditis, vasculitis, papillitis), panuveitis. Always check corneal sensation (low in HSV/VZV, leprosy) and IOP (high in HSV, VZV, CMV, toxo, syphilis, sarcoid, Posner-Schlossman). Granulomatous = mutton-fat KPs, iris nodules (Koeppe margin, Busacca stroma, Berlin angle) → infection, sarcoid, VKH, sympathetic ophthalmia, lens-induced, MS.
points: Stellate KPs all over the endothelium: HSV, VZV, CMV, toxo, Fuchs, sarcoid.
Hypopyon uveitis: HLA-B27 (West), Behçet (Asia).
Sectoral iris atrophy = herpetic; diffuse = Fuchs.
chunks.hook: Uveitis exam = sensation, pressure, KPs, iris, fundus — every time.

cards.q: Koeppe vs Busacca nodules?
cards.a: Koeppe at the pupillary margin; Busacca in the iris stroma (both granulomatous).

cards.q: Uveitis causes with raised IOP?
cards.a: HSV, VZV, CMV, toxoplasmosis, syphilis, sarcoidosis, Posner-Schlossman.

chunks.title: Work-up, complications & treatment
chunks.tldr: First mild unilateral non-granulomatous AAU that responds → no tests. Recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous, intermediate/posterior/pan, or non-responding → test syphilis (VDRL/RPR + treponemal FTA-ABS), TB (CXR + PPD or IGRA), sarcoid (CXR, ACE, lysozyme); then tailored (HLA-B27, ANA in JIA, toxo serology). Complications: synechiae → iris bombé/angle closure, cataract, glaucoma, CME, RD (exudative = VKH, SO, posterior scleritis). Rx: prednisolone acetate 1% hourly-2 hourly (shake it!) + cycloplegic (homatropine); posterior → sub-Tenon triamcinolone 40 mg, intravitreal, oral prednisone 0.5–1.5 mg/kg; steroid-sparers (MTX, MMF, aza, cyclosporine, anti-TNF).
points: Cataract surgery only after ≥3–6 months quiet, with steroid cover.
Rule out epithelial defect/open globe and herpes before steroids.
chunks.hook: Every uveitis work-up: Syphilis, TB, Sarcoid — the great imitators.

cards.q: Three tests ordered in almost every non-trivial uveitis?
cards.a: Syphilis serology (treponemal + non-treponemal), TB (CXR + IGRA/PPD), sarcoid (CXR, ACE/lysozyme).

cards.q: Why give a cycloplegic in anterior uveitis?
cards.a: Relieves ciliary spasm pain and prevents posterior synechiae.

chunks.title: HLA-B27 & JIA uveitis
chunks.tldr: HLA-B27 AAU: men, acute unilateral alternating, fibrin/hypopyon, non-granulomatous; HLA-B27 in ~50–90% of AAU; half develop systemic disease — ankylosing spondylitis (up to 50% get uveitis), reactive arthritis, IBD, psoriatic arthritis. JIA: girls 4–5:1, oligoarticular, ANA+; chronic, white, painless bilateral iridocyclitis found at 5–6 y by screening — band keratopathy, synechiae, cataract, glaucoma, CME. Rx topical steroid, then MTX, adalimumab; IOL often avoided.
points: Uveitis may precede arthritis by years; knee commonest joint.
JIA kids need regular slitlamp screening because they don't complain.
chunks.hook: JIA eye is quiet and white — damage happens silently.

cards.q: Highest-risk JIA group for uveitis?
cards.a: Young girls with oligoarticular (pauciarticular) JIA who are ANA positive.

cards.q: Systemic diseases linked to HLA-B27 anterior uveitis?
cards.a: Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis (Reiter), inflammatory bowel disease, psoriatic arthritis.

chunks.title: Fuchs heterochromic & lens-induced uveitis
chunks.tldr: Fuchs uveitis syndrome: 3rd–4th decade, unilateral, painless, white; heterochromia (affected eye usually lighter), diffuse stellate KPs, iris stromal atrophy, no posterior synechiae, angle vessels (Amsler sign = bleed on paracentesis), vitritis; cataract in most, glaucoma 10–15%. Don't over-treat with steroids; cataract surgery does well. Lens-induced (phacoantigenic): immune reaction to leaked lens protein (hypermature cataract, trauma, retained fragments); phacolytic glaucoma — cure = remove lens material.
points: In dark irides, Fuchs eye looks lighter; in blue irides it can paradoxically look darker.

cards.q: What is Amsler's sign?
cards.a: Filiform haemorrhage from fragile angle vessels during AC paracentesis/surgery in Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis.

chunks.title: Intermediate uveitis & clues to posterior uveitis
chunks.tldr: Intermediate: young adults, bilateral ~80%, floaters; snowballs/snowbanking, peripheral vasculitis; exclude sarcoid, MS, syphilis, TB. Vision lost from CME and PSC. Treat CME: topical steroid trial 3–4 wk (steroid responder?) → sub-Tenon/intravitreal triamcinolone. Posterior uveitis clues by age: <3 y masquerades (RB, leukaemia), congenital infections; 4–15 y toxo, toxocara; 16–50 syphilis, TB, sarcoid, toxo, Behçet, VKH, ARN; >50 add lymphoma, birdshot, endophthalmitis. Unilateral: toxo, toxocara, ARN, endogenous infection.
points: Commonest retinitis (immunocompetent): toxo, syphilis, Behçet. Commonest choroiditis: sarcoid, TB, VKH.
Little vitritis: serpiginous, POHS. Heavy vitritis: toxo, bacterial endophthalmitis.
Papillitis with painful eye movements → MS; macular star → Bartonella.
chunks.hook: Snowballs in a young adult — ask about neuro symptoms (MS).

cards.q: Most common cause of visual loss in intermediate uveitis?
cards.a: Cystoid macular oedema (then posterior subcapsular cataract).

chunks.title: Toxoplasmosis, POHS & toxocariasis
chunks.tldr: Toxo (cats; oocysts, undercooked meat, congenital): fluffy white focal retinochoroiditis next to an old pigmented scar, dense vitritis ('headlight in fog'). Small peripheral lesion → observe. Threatening → pyrimethamine (75 mg load ×2 d then 25–50 mg/d) + sulfadiazine + folinic acid ×4–6 wk; or TMP-SMX, clindamycin. Oral steroids only under antimicrobial cover; no periocular depot steroid. POHS (Ohio-Mississippi): punched-out spots, peripapillary atrophy, no vitritis, CNV → anti-VEGF. Toxocara (pica, puppies): unilateral child, posterior pole or peripheral granuloma, chronic endophthalmitis, leukocoria; ELISA; steroids ± vitrectomy, no anthelmintic.
points: Weekly FBC on pyrimethamine.
Visceral larva migrans ~2 y with eosinophilia; ocular ~7 y without.
chunks.hook: New white lesion hugging an old black scar = toxo.

cards.q: Classic triple therapy for ocular toxoplasmosis?
cards.a: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid (± oral prednisolone after 24–48 h).

cards.q: Why avoid anthelmintics in ocular toxocariasis?
cards.a: Killing the larva may worsen intraocular inflammation.

chunks.title: AIDS, TB, sarcoid & syphilis uveitis
chunks.tldr: AIDS: CD4 <100 → CMV retinitis ('pizza-pie' haemorrhagic geographic necrosis; 30–40% pre-HAART); VZV/HSV progress faster; consider toxo, syphilis, crypto, lymphoma. TB: granulomatous KPs, choroidal tubercles; 4-drug therapy 6–9 months. Sarcoid: 25% of systemic sarcoid get uveitis; granulomatous, candle-wax periphlebitis, black patients; CXR hilar nodes, ACE, lysozyme, biopsy non-caseating granuloma; Heerfordt (uveoparotid), Mikulicz. Syphilis (secondary/tertiary): any uveitis, ground-glass placoid retinitis, papillitis; VDRL can be falsely negative late → do treponemal test; LP; IV penicillin G 4 MU 4-hourly ×14 d.
points: Treat syphilitic uveitis as neurosyphilis.

cards.q: Treatment for syphilitic uveitis?
cards.a: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 4 million units IV every 4 h for 14 days (neurosyphilis regimen).

cards.q: Fundus sign of sarcoid vasculitis?
cards.a: Candle-wax drippings (periphlebitis with exudates).

chunks.title: Sympathetic ophthalmia & tropical uveitis
chunks.tldr: Sympathetic ophthalmia: bilateral granulomatous panuveitis 10 days–years (90% within 1 y) after penetrating injury (rarely surgery); exciting eye then sympathising eye; Dalen-Fuchs nodules, exudative RD. Prevent: enucleate a blind, badly injured eye within ~10 days. Treat: high-dose steroids (1–1.5 mg/kg) + steroid-sparers. Leptospirosis: farmers/rat urine, fever, hypopyon panuveitis + vasculitis; penicillin/doxycycline. Onchocerciasis (river blindness, black fly): microfilariae in AC, sclerosing keratitis, chorioretinitis; ivermectin + nodulectomy. Cysticercosis: intravitreal/subretinal cyst with scolex → vitrectomy.
points: Untreated sympathetic ophthalmia → bilateral blindness.
chunks.hook: Injured eye blind? Remove it within 2 weeks to save the other.

cards.q: What are Dalen-Fuchs nodules?
cards.a: Yellow-white deep nodules of epithelioid cells between RPE and Bruch's — seen in sympathetic ophthalmia (and VKH).

cards.q: Drug of choice for onchocerciasis?
cards.a: Ivermectin (single dose 150–200 µg/kg, repeated 6–12-monthly).

chunks.title: Benign uveal tumours
chunks.tldr: Nevus: common in older whites (2–10%); flat grey-brown, feathery edge, drusen on surface (dormant); 95% <5 mm/<1 mm. Melanocytoma: jet-black lesion on the disc. Circumscribed choroidal haemangioma: orange-red dome near disc/macula, 30s–40s; ICG early fill + late washout; US high internal reflectivity; Rx PDT. Diffuse haemangioma: 'tomato-ketchup' fundus in Sturge-Weber, glaucoma. Choroidal osteoma: young women, orange-white peripapillary plate, CNV risk; bone on US/CT.
points: Suspicious features in a pigmented lesion: thickness >2 mm, orange pigment, subretinal fluid, symptoms, margin near disc, growth — 'TFSOM'.
chunks.hook: Drusen on top = old & sleepy; orange pigment + fluid = waking up.

cards.q: ICG pattern of circumscribed choroidal haemangioma?
cards.a: Early intense hyperfluorescence with late 'washout' of the centre.

cards.q: Diffuse choroidal haemangioma is a feature of which syndrome?
cards.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome (with facial port-wine stain).

chunks.title: Uveal melanoma
chunks.tldr: Commonest primary adult intraocular malignancy; whites, light irides, ocular melanocytosis, dysplastic nevus syndrome. Iris (40s): nodular, vessels, pupil peaking, ectropion, angle seeding → glaucoma; best prognosis. Ciliary body: sentinel vessels, lens indentation; worst. Choroid: dome or collar-stud/mushroom (through Bruch's); US low internal reflectivity, choroidal excavation. Metastasis → liver. Bad prognosis: large, ciliary body, epithelioid cells, monosomy 3, GEP class 2. Rx: plaque brachytherapy (I-125/Ru-106) or proton beam; enucleation for large/disc-involving; iris → excision or plaque.
points: COMS: medium tumours — I-125 plaque = enucleation for survival; pre-enucleation EBRT for large tumours no benefit.
Metastatic disease: median survival short; no adjuvant proven.
chunks.hook: Melanoma spreads to the Liver — check LFTs/imaging for life.

cards.q: Chromosomal marker of high metastatic risk in uveal melanoma?
cards.a: Monosomy 3 (and GEP class 2, BAP1 loss).

cards.q: Key COMS finding for medium choroidal melanoma?
cards.a: Iodine-125 plaque brachytherapy gives the same survival as enucleation.

chunks.title: Uveal metastasis & lymphoid lesions
chunks.tldr: Metastasis is the most common intraocular malignancy. Sources: breast (women), lung (men), colon. Choroid: creamy-yellow plaque/dome, subretinal fluid out of proportion, multifocal/bilateral in ~20%, grows in weeks. Treat as brain metastasis (~20% have CNS mets): palliative EBRT/chemo; median survival ~6 months. Atypical lymphoid hyperplasia & primary uveal lymphoma: creamy diffuse choroidal infiltrates, salmon epibulbar mass; biopsy; low-dose EBRT; 20% develop systemic lymphoma (unlike vitreoretinal lymphoma, which goes to brain).
chunks.hook: Creamy choroidal mass in a woman — check the breasts.

cards.q: Commonest primary sites for uveal metastasis?
cards.a: Breast in women, lung in men (then GI).

chunks.title: Episcleritis vs scleritis
chunks.tldr: Episcleritis: young women, sudden redness, mild discomfort, simple or nodular, vessels blanch with phenylephrine and move; self-limits 1–2 wk; tears, topical steroid, oral NSAID if recurrent. Scleritis: ~48 y, severe boring pain radiating to face/jaw, waking at night; violaceous deep vessels; up to 2/3 systemic disease — RA, GPA, relapsing polychondritis, PAN, SLE, IBD; infections (zoster, TB, post-surgical Pseudomonas). Types: diffuse, nodular, necrotising (worst), scleromalacia perforans (painless, RA, old women), posterior (choroidal folds, exudative RD, proptosis, disc swelling; T-sign on US).
points: Diffuse/nodular: oral NSAID (indomethacin 75 mg, flurbiprofen) → oral steroid if no response in 2 wk.
Necrotising: prednisolone 1 mg/kg, IV methylpred, cyclophosphamide (GPA), rituximab/anti-TNF.
Topical steroid alone doesn't control scleritis. SINS = surgically induced necrotising scleritis.
chunks.hook: Pain that wakes you at night + purple eye = scleritis; look for vasculitis.

cards.q: Ultrasound sign of posterior scleritis?
cards.a: Scleral thickening with fluid in sub-Tenon's space (T-sign).

cards.q: Which scleritis is painless?
cards.a: Scleromalacia perforans (usually long-standing RA).

chunks.title: Scleral thinning & thickening
chunks.tldr: Ectasia = sclera stretched alone; staphyloma = sclera + uvea bulge (anterior/ciliary/intercalary, equatorial, posterior in pathological myopia). Scleral coloboma inferior to disc with uveal/retinal coloboma; buphthalmos from infantile glaucoma. Blue sclera in OI, Ehlers-Danlos. Nanophthalmos: tiny eye, thick sclera, high hyperopia → angle closure and uveal effusion (risky surgery).
chunks.hook: Small eye, thick sclera = beware angle closure and effusions.

cards.q: Two complications of nanophthalmos?
cards.a: Angle-closure glaucoma and uveal effusion syndrome (especially with intraocular surgery).
